profile.summary: This is Rewire's own study, not a third-party suite. One Evo 2 7B container image, pinned by digest, scored the 3,893 BRCA1 single nucleotide variants of the Findlay et al. saturation genome editing table on three cloud GPUs, and the resulting zero-shot loss-of-function scores were compared with CADD, mammalian phyloP and a consequence rule on the same variants. Alongside the AUROCs it records what each run cost, how much GPU memory it used, how fast it scored, and whether different hardware gives the same per-variant numbers. It answers an operational question rather than a biological one: can this model be run reproducibly on commercial clouds, and does the hardware change the answer.

summary_quotes.text: Can one pinned Evo 2 7B workload (sequence scoring, paired variant windows and embedding extraction) be run reproducibly on single-GPU instances on AWS, Google Cloud and a GPU cloud?
Findlay et al. 2018 BRCA1 saturation genome editing table: 3,893 SNVs with functional class (FUNC 2,821, INT 249, LOF 823), consequence, CADD score and mammalian phyloP.

No new biological claim is made. Variant scores are not a calibrated clinical interpretation.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Three things at once. First, whether a pinned Evo 2 7B workload runs at all on each platform, gated by a correctness test that reproduces Arc's expected forward-pass loss of 0.3476563 within 0.001. Second, how well the model's zero-shot score separates loss-of-function from functional BRCA1 variants, overall and split into coding and noncoding, against three baselines that need no GPU. Third, the operational facts a clinical informatician would ask for: GPU memory, wall time, throughput, cost, and whether two machines give the same per-variant score. The authors state the point of the study is an executable recipe rather than another benchmark.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Everything is pinned and public. The container is built from NVIDIA's PyTorch 25.04 image with evo2 0.6.0 and vtx 1.1.0 and referenced by digest; the weights are Hugging Face revisions with SHA-256 checks before loading, which the authors require because Arc's loader uses pickle; the inputs come from a pinned Arc commit and are hash-checked rather than redistributed. The variant set is the Findlay et al. 2018 BRCA1 saturation genome editing table: 3,893 single nucleotide variants labelled FUNC (2,821), INT (249) or LOF (823), with consequence, a CADD score and mammalian phyloP in the same table. W1 scores each variant in an 8,192 base pair window centred on it, as the Arc notebook does, taking the variant's mean log-likelihood minus the reference's. Labels are LOF against FUNC plus INT.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: AUROC of the negated score, with 95% intervals from 2,000 bootstrap resamples at seed 7, resampling positions and keeping the three variants at a position together. Each baseline is compared with Evo 2 by a paired bootstrap difference in AUROC with its own interval, and no significance threshold is applied. Cross-platform agreement is measured against a reference platform as the maximum and median absolute difference in per-variant scores, the Spearman correlation, and how many variants move more than 1% of the list in rank; W4 repeats the first 200 variants in a second process on the same machine to separate run-to-run from cross-hardware variation. Each platform runs once from a clean committed revision with the same image digest, outputs are committed as evidence, and failed attempts are kept. results.json holds only scientific outputs; timings and costs live in operations.json and are not compared.

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: Evo 2 7B reached AUROC 0.875 (95% CI 0.859 to 0.891) over all 3,893 variants, 0.840 on coding and 0.953 on noncoding. Against the baselines in the same table, the paired differences favour Evo 2 overall (CADD 0.804, phyloP 0.781, consequence rule 0.769), but on coding variants the difference against CADD is -0.0008 with an interval from -0.026 to 0.023, so no advantage is detected there, while on noncoding the advantage holds against all three. The two H100 platforms, on different clouds, produced identical scores (maximum absolute difference 0.0, Spearman 1.0), while the L40S differed (maximum 1.3e-3, median 1.2e-4, Spearman 0.983) and its AUROC came out at 0.877 instead of 0.875. Each platform repeated its own scores exactly. Throughput was 2.93 sequences per second on the Google Cloud H100 and 2.91 on the Runpod H100, against 0.61 on the L40S, with peak W1 GPU memory of about 16.8 GiB and costs of USD 4.78, 2.82 and 2.96 for the run.

sections.title: The amendment 7 follow-up
sections.body: A later analysis, planned in advance and run without a GPU, asks whether the noncoding advantage holds against current predictors rather than the CADD v1.3 column shipped with the Findlay table. It adds CADD v1.7 for GRCh37, SpliceAI as annotated in that CADD release, and REVEL for missense variants, scored on the same variants and labels with the same grouped bootstrap, and fixes in advance what counts as an advantage holding: the 95% interval of the paired difference above zero. The repository reports the answer as no: against CADD v1.3 the noncoding advantage holds, against CADD v1.7 and SpliceAI it is not detected, and on coding and missense variants CADD v1.7 and REVEL lead. The amendment also states in advance that CADD v1.7 uses SpliceAI as a feature so the two are not independent, and that REVEL may be optimistic on BRCA1 because its training data may include these variants.
sections.source_locator: amendment-007.md: Question, Inputs, Analysis, Caveats stated in advance. README.md: Main findings

quotes.text: On the same 3,893 BRCA1 SNVs and labels as W1, how do current CADD, SpliceAI and (for missense variants) REVEL compare with Evo 2 7B? In particular, does Evo 2's noncoding advantage hold?
Evo 2's advantage over a predictor "holds" in a region if the 95% interval of the paired difference (Evo 2 minus predictor) is above 0, "reverses" if below 0, and is "not detected" otherwise.

Evo 2's noncoding advantage holds against CADD v1.3 only. Against CADD v1.7 and SpliceAI it is not detected (AUROC 0.953 against 0.932 and 0.963), and on coding and missense variants CADD v1.7 and REVEL lead.
CADD v1.7 uses SpliceAI among its features, so CADD v1.7 and SpliceAI are not independent.
REVEL was trained on disease and putatively neutral missense variants from HGMD and population data, which may include BRCA1 variants, so its BRCA1 performance may be optimistic.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository is the deliverable: a make target runs the offline input fetch, hash checks and tests, and one orchestration command launches a platform, runs the pinned image and assembles results. Each launcher creates a machine with a one-off SSH key and a three-hour limit, copies the committed code and inputs, runs the image, copies results back and deletes the machine whatever happens. Credentials are kept outside the repository and the provider quotas needed are listed. Note what this costs: scoring ran at USD 0.45 to 0.80 per 1,000 variants at October 2026 list prices, and at least 100 GB of disk is needed because the image is about 25 GB unpacked and the two 7B checkpoints are 13.8 GB and 13.0 GB.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One variant set plus two small auxiliary sets. BRCA1: the Findlay et al. 2018 saturation genome editing table, 3,893 single nucleotide variants labelled FUNC 2,821, INT 249 and LOF 823, with consequence, CADD score and mammalian phyloP in the same file. Also chromosome 17 of GRCh37 as the sequence context, 122 labelled exon and non-exon positions from Arc's exon classifier notebook, Arc's four forward-pass test sequences, and synthetic DNA generated from seed 20261007 for the memory probe.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: There is none: the model is used zero-shot, so every one of the 3,893 variants is scored and included in the AUROC. The only partitions are for reporting: coding (missense, nonsense, synonymous) against noncoding (all other consequences), and in the bootstrap, resampling by genomic position so that the three variants at a position stay together.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC of the negated Evo 2 score for LOF against FUNC plus INT, higher better, with 95% bootstrap intervals and paired differences against each baseline. The exon workload reports AUROC on 122 positions. The operational measures are sequences per second and peak GPU memory, plus wall times and cost in US dollars; agreement is reported as maximum and median absolute score difference, Spearman correlation and rank movement.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Little is possible and the study says so. Evo 2 7B is used zero-shot on a published variant table, and nothing is stated about whether BRCA1 or these variants appear in the model's pretraining data. Where a control was impossible the study marks the result as a demonstration rather than an evaluation: the exon classifier's training data may include the 122 positions, so that workload is labelled a pipeline demonstration. Amendment 7 records in advance that REVEL's training data may include BRCA1 variants, and that CADD v1.7 and SpliceAI are not independent of each other.

run_guide.summary: Prepare and verify the inputs offline, then run one platform's workloads from the pinned container image and let the launcher tear the machine down.
prerequisites: Local tools uv, jq, ssh, and the gcloud or aws CLI for those providers.
Provider access: Google Cloud quota of at least 1 preemptible H100, or Runpod prepaid credit; AWS needs On-Demand P and G instance quota and is untested in this study.
Credentials kept outside the repository, for example in ~/.config/evo2ops/env with mode 600.
At least 100 GB of disk: the image is about 25 GB unpacked and the two 7B checkpoints are 13.8 GB and 13.0 GB; the launchers use 200 GB.
Money: scoring cost USD 0.45 to 0.80 per 1,000 variants at October 2026 list prices, and the study's own cap was USD 150.
Licence terms: Evo 2 code and weights are Apache-2.0, the Findlay et al. BRCA1 function scores are free for nonprofit use only, and the study code's licence is stated as to be set at publication.

notes: Written from five files of the public rewire-bio/evo2-cloud-operations repository at commit f8ae11c9a1c45505487c978b4cb7e064c4e59905, which are the five sources already on the record. Points for a human. First, the platform identifiers moved between the protocol and the run: the protocol lists P1 to P4 with P1 (AWS H100) as the reference platform, while results.json records P1 and P4 as unavailable, P2, P3 and P5 as completed, and P2 (Google Cloud H100) as the reference platform; P5, the Runpod L40S, does not appear in the protocol's platform table at all. Second, the AUROC values in brca1_evo2_vs_baselines match P2 and P3 exactly; P5's differ (0.877 against 0.875 overall), so any figure quoted from this study carries its GPU with it. Third, sizes: 3,893 is the whole set, 2,086 the missense count stated in amendment 7, but the missense comparison runs only on missense variants scored by REVEL, whose count no file read gives, and no file read gives the coding or noncoding counts, so those three entries have size null. Fourth, the throughput entry's figure is the Google Cloud H100's 2.9297 sequences per second; the Runpod H100 recorded 2.9075 and the L40S 0.6117, and costs for the run were USD 4.78, 2.82 and 2.96 respectively. Fifth, the study code has no licence yet (the README says it is to be set at publication, and the GitHub API reports none), the input function scores are nonprofit use only, and no per-variant scores are committed, so the source files are kept but not stored. Sixth, the amendment 7 numbers quoted here come from the README's summary; the follow-up results file itself was not fetched.
